Arpeggiator 4 Step:
Arpeggiator 4 Step: A fun little preset that sets up an arpeggiated Phase Generator sequence using four (Control) controls changing pitches. The arpeggiation is created by changing Shape generators that successively trigger each other in a circle starting off with a seed generator to begin the pattern. Formulas V,T,R, and P map to each SG with a fast steep down amplitude ramp to generate a volume shape for each of four distinct Phase generators. The slower you set the speed the more the Phase generator will ring out. At a faster speed it has a plucked string sound that you can vary the timbre of a bit using the Spread control. A good preset to show you have to can use one Shape Generator to trigger another in succession.

Macro i (Pitch.1): Sets Phase generator one to one of 13 semitone pitches.
Macro ii (Pitch.2): Sets Phase generator two to one of 13 semitone pitches.
Macro iii (Pitch.3): Sets Phase generator three to one of 13 semitone pitches.
Macro iv (Pitch.4): Sets Phase generator four to one of 13 semitone pitches.

v: Increases Frequency Spread of the Phase Generators for timbral change that is more of a different plucking timbre at higher speeds.
vi: Increases speed of the arpeggiated pattern.
 
X: Pitch, and triggers the start of an arpeggiator
Y: Pitch/timing offset. Bottom Y = At pitch. Middle Y = Octave higher, last third of Y Y = up an octave and a fifth, and at twice arpeggiator speed.
Z: Volume 

Ped 1: iii (change as desired to any of i, ii, iii or iv). Note the Min/Max settings for this pedal. It's been set so that the control goes from pitch 4 (major third) to pitch 5 (major fourth).
Ped 2: vi (base speed of arpeggiation).

Note 1: Pressing more than one finger at a time will trigger multiple arpeggiators each with their own starting point. At a lower speed, try pressing two or three finger slightly offset in time to get a variety of interesting patterns.

Note 2: Connect up an external controller device like a SoftStep to change multiple CCs simultaneously to trigger chord changes.

Note 3: You can change the Phase generators to Oscillators if you wish for a different timbre.

Audio Through:
Audio Through: The simplest of presets that just sends the Stereo Analog Audio input directly to SL/SR out the master section.

Intended for EaganMatrix Module use. Although it is simple it allows you to apply Recirculator and Tilt EQ to whatever analog input you send the module. 
 
Controls: None

X: Not used
Y: Not used
Z: Not used

EaganMatrix Module Tip: Tee preset uses the default Recirculator "Reverb". You can adjust the Reverb Level/Mix and Reverb Decay in the Menu system. Press the "Oct -" and "Oct +" buttons together and then "Oct +" to move to "EfL nn" to adjust the Effect Level with the rotary to the desired value. The preset loads dry (value = 0). the next menu option "EfT" will adjust the Effect Time with the rotary. Press the two octave buttons again to exit the menu system which will leave the leaves as is but note they will return to the original values if you go to another preset and back so if you have a setting you like, save the preset to a User Preset slot for later use.

You can also adjust the Tilt EQ settings in the menu system with the "EqT" (Tilt), "EqF" (Frequency) and "EqL" (Level)settings.

Other things to try:
In the editor you can change the type of recirculator to "Modulated Delay", "Swept Echo", "Analog Echo", "Digital Echo with LPF" and "Digital Echo with HFP" options. Save the preset to a User Preset slot or save to disk for later recall. You can adjust "EfL" and "EfT" for these as you did for the default Reverb option.

Note that the three additional Recirculator controls "R1", "R2" and "R3" cannot be accessed from the module but you can change them in the editor or using a Midi controller change them with Midi CC21 and CC22. Complete Midi CC Controls for the Recirculator and EQ are as follows. Note that R1, R2 and R3 have different functions depending on the Recirculator type loaded.

CC20: Recirculator R1 Control - Diffuse, ModDepth, LPF, HPF
CC21: Recirculator R2 Control - Darkness, ModRate, Offset
CC22: Recirculator R3 Control - Damping, Feedback
CC23: Recirculator R4 Control - Decay, Time (Same as EfT)
CC24: Recirculator Mix Control - (Same as EfL)
CC83: EQ Tilt Control (Same as EqT)
CC84: EQ Frequency Control (Same as EqF)
CC85: EQ Level/Mix Control (Same as EqL)

You can also turn on Extended Recirculation in the editor and save the preset with that setting. The "Extend" control runs the filter at a lower sample rate - can double the effective max delay time. This means the "wet" part of the signal contains only lower frequencies (below the half sample rate), and you have to mix in "dry" to get more highs. In many cases, this sounds pretty natural -- there are many reverb effects which don't do much with highs and work well with "extend".

First define a Master Oscillator (DSF OSC, INT OSC or Phase Generator) and then define one or more Jenny Oscillators to the right of it (typically one or two are used but three basic types are defined in this preset so you can hear the difference).

BiqBank - Basic:
Basic Biqbank: A basic preset for learning the Biquad Filter Bank (BiqBank) function and a building block for more complex presets that use it. This preset sends steep slope (48 dB /Oct)low pass filtered noise into the BiqBank. Operating on noise is a very common use case.

BiqBank Note: A set of biquad bandpass filters. BiqBank provides bandpass filters on an audio-rate input, with filter parameters controlled by the matrix as described in the table above. Each BiqBank may consist of 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, or 48 bandpass filters. The indicator above the first BiqBank matrix column is off for Normal (8 bandpass filters), on for Extended (16, 24, 32, 40, or 48 bandpass filters). Click on the Indicator to change its state.

The Deflation Limit (above the last BiqBank matrix column) avoids excessive buildup of energy inside the BiqBank, but has no effect under normal playing conditions. Set the Deflation Limit to the largest value (between 0 and 7) that does not affect the timbre of the sound. Click on the Deflation Limit to change its value.

Note that it is common to send a single pulse of noise into a BiqBank that will fade. Here a constant noise source is fed into it and you need to be careful not to saturate the filter at too low a bandwidth that will make it ring out of control. This preset lets you set Bandwidth to zero for experimentation which it someting that you likely will not do too often in practice. Turn down the gain to be safe and then experiment with each Control to hear what that does to BiqBank filtered noise. Also try changing sF and sB to the quadratic options qF and qB to hear how that affects the sound.

Macro i (sF-qSF): Frequency Spread (or Quadradic Spread Frequency). sF; 1 for harmonic spacing of bandpass filters, >1 for stretched spacing, <1 for compressed spacing. qF; 0 for harmonic spacing, >0 for offsets proportional to harmonic-numbersquared.
Macro ii (B): BandPass Bandwidth Control. Bandpass bandwidth control, smaller values increase resonance
Macro iii (sB-qsB): Spread Bandwidth (or Quadratic Spread Bandwidth).sB linear, qB quadratic by mode number. 0 means each mode has the same bandwidth, >0 means modes farther from Centre (C column) have increased bandwidth, <0 means modes farther from Centre have decreased bandwidth.
Macro iv (C): Center Control. 0 means first bandpass filter is Centre, 1 means 8th bandpass filter is Centre.

v (sA): Amplitude Spread. 0 for uniform amplitude bandpass filters, >0 reduced amplitude farther from
Centre.
vi (In Freq): Cutoff frequency of the low pass filer that feeds noise into the BiqBank.

X: BiqBank Frequency. Frequency (in kHz) for the first bandpass filter in the BiqBank.
Y: Not Used
Z: Volume + Tone (affects BiqGraph Bandwidth).

BiqGraph - Basic:
Basic BiqGraph:  A basic preset to experiment with the BiqGraph filter. The BiqGraph is a variant on the BiqBank that allows you to specify a base harmonic amplitude control graph applied to an audio input and then specify two sets of amplitude offsets that can be applied under program control (also one set of frequency graph offsets and one set of Bandwidth graph adjustments are available if amplitude adjustments are not desired). This allow you to perform very fine harmonic and frequency manipulation to any sound. Obviously sounds rich in harmonics will provide the best sonic canvas on which to perform this spectral painting.

X: Control BiqGraph Frequency parameter. Frequency (in kHz) for the first mode in the BiqGraph
Y: Not Used
Z: Volume 

Macro i (FreqSprd): Frequeny Spread. 1 for harmonic spacing of modes, >1 stretched harmonics, <1 compressed.

Macro ii (ModeBand): Bandwodth. Bandwidth control, smaller values increase mode resonance

Macro iii (ModeSprd): Mode Bandwidth Spread. means each mode has the same bandwidth, >0 means higher modes have increasing bandwidth, <0 higher modes have decreasing bandwidth.

Control v (OddHarms): 1A Graph Control. Controls applying the 1A amplitude offset graph that emphasizes odd harmonics and reduces even harmonics. A more clarinet-like sound will result as you bring this in when applied to the base sawtooth input. Scale factor for 1 Graph, offsetting Mode dB Amplitudes. If set 1F: Scale factor for 1 Graph, offsetting Mode % Frequencies

Control vi (EvenHarms): 2A Graph Control. Controls applying the 2A amplitude offset graph that emphasizes even harmonics and reduces odd harmonics. A more nasal brassy-like sound will result as you bring this in when applied to the base sawtooth input. Scale factor for 2 Graph, offsetting Mode dB Amplitudes. If set 2B: Scale factor for 2 Graph, offsetting Mode dB Bandwidth

Notes for BiqGraph:
BiqBank, BiqGraph, BiqMouth, and ModMan are four different ways to control the same underlying technology: a set of biquad bandpass filters. BiqGraph is suitable for Modal Physical Modeling. In Modal Modeling terminology, each biquad bandpass filter is called a "mode". The amplitudes for each mode are computed from dB amplitude values specified in three amplitude graphs. The three graphs are called A Graph (dB amplitude values), 1 Graph (first set of dB amplitude offsets), and 2 Graph (second set of dB amplitude offsets). These graphs are combined under control of matrix
columns, resulting in time-varying mode amplitudes, as explained on the next page. Alternatively, by selecting 1F instead of 1A for the matrix column, the 1 Graph may be used for Scaled %
Frequency Offsets. By selecting 2B instead of 2A for the matrix column, the 2 Graph may be used for Scaled dB Bandwidth Offsets.

Each BiqGraph may consist of 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, or 48 modes. The indicator above the first BiqGraph matrix column is off for Normal (8 modes), on for Extended (16, 24, 32, 40, or 48 modes). Click on the Indicator to change its state. 

The Deflation Limit (above the last BiqGraph matrix column) avoids excessive buildup of energy inside the BiqGraph, but has no effect under normal playing conditions. Set the Deflation Limit to the largest value (between 0 and 7) that does not affect the timbre of the sound. Click on the Deflation Limit to change its value. BiqGraph Graphs: Click on the the word Graph to inspect and edit three graphs: Mode Amplitudes (A graph)  first set of dB amplitude offsets (1 Graph), and second set of dB amplitude offsets (2 Graph). The dB amplitude of each of the modes is computed from the Mode Amplitude A graph, plus matrix column 1A times the 1 Graph, plus matrix column 2A times the
2 Graph.

The Basic BiqGraph preset uses a Sawtooth Wavebank to input a full spectrum sound into the BiqGraph which sets a descending harmonic amplitude graph (similar to the harmonic structure of the sawtooth wave). Then two sets of amplitude offsets are defined - the first emphasizing the odd harmonics and the second emphasizing the even harmonics.

Experiment with the input contol graph and offsets graphs to hear what changing them does. BUT BE CARE HERE AS YOU CAN EASILY OVERLOAD HARMONICS IF YOU SET THEM TOO HIGH AND THE DOUNS CAN BREAK UP - SO ALWAYS TURN DOWN THE GAIN BEFORE EXPERIMENTING WITH BIQUAD FILTERS.

Examples of BiqGraph usage in EaganMatrix System Presets:
French Sax: Uses an Oscillator as a waveshaper in a BiqGraph feedback loop, to create a cross between a sax and harmonica.
Slide Wind EM: Uses an Oscillator as a waveshaper in a BiqGraph feedback loop, to create a changing-body-size wind instrument.
Space Flute: Uses an Oscillator as a waveshaper in a BiqGraph feedback loop, to create a flute-like sound with spacey echo repeats.
BiqMouth - Basic:
Basic BiqMouth: A basic preset for experimenting with the BiqMouth vocal formant generator. A Sawtooth WaveBank with fur waves using small frequency offsets and variable phased sine LFO on each wave (speed based on pressure)is sent into a BiqMouth with controls set for each of the parameters. Note that the formant generator typically sounds best when sent a signal that has a full and complex harmonic spectrum. A sawtooth wave has a full spectrum of this nature. If you set to Square or Triangle the vocal quality you want will not be possible if the goal to try and emulate the voice. Modulated waveforms also can work well as BiqBank inputs if the spectrum is full ad rich.

The BiqMouth takes an audio input that may have to be scaled based on the amplitude of the signal being passed. If you get a buzzing sound on playing, try reducing the input into the BiqMouth (or any biquad filter bank under similar buzzing/overloading conditions).

BiqBank, BiqGraph, BiqMouth, and ModMan are four different ways to control the same underlying technology: a set of biquad bandpass filters. BiqMouth is suitable for vocal filtering of an audio-rate input. In voice modeling terminology, each biquad bandpass filter is called a "formant". The matrix columns control the parameters of 5 formants, to simulate a variety of mouth shapes.

Each mouth shape is implemented using 5 vocal formants. Five biquad bandpass filters are set at the appropriate frequencies, amplitudes, and bandwidths to imitate the resonances of the mouth shape. The Deflation Limit (above the last BiqMouth matrix column) avoids excessive buildup of energy inside the BiqMouth, but has no effect under normal playing conditions. Set the Deflation Limit to the largest value (between 0 and 7) that does not affect the timbre of the sound. Click on the Deflation Limit to change its value.

Macro ii (FreqMult): Multiplier on formant frequencies, "1.0" = normal.
Macro iii (Offset): Offset on formant frequencies, "0.0" (blank column) = normal.
Macro iv (BandMult): Formant bandwidth multiplier, "1.0" means each formant has default bandwidth, > "1.0" means formants farther from Centre (see below) have increased bandwidth, < "1.0" means formants farther from Centre have decreased bandwidth.

v(Center): BiqMouth Centre control, 0 means first formant is center, "0.625" means last (5th) formant is center.
vi(AmpSpread): BiqMouth amplitude spread, 0 means no amplitude scaling of formants, > 0 means reduced amplitude of formants farther from Centre.

Creaker:
Creaker: Two Oscillators are phase modulated by formula controlled shape generator phase modulation and sent through high pass filters with cutoff frequencies an octave multiple apart and then to opposite stereo channels. 

Note 1: The high pass filters are both set to cascade 3 (red number under "HPr"). Try changing the cascading of the filters to different values. At the "single filter" setting you will hear more low frequency content.

Note 2: The "creaking" is derived from the over modulation of the two oscillators (formulas "A" and "C") and passing only the high frequency component of that through the filters. Notice the cutoff of the two filers are multiplied by constants of "4" and "8" respectively. You will get a more perceived pitch content if you reduce these multipliers to let more of the low frequency end through (try changing the "4" and "8" in the "F" column of he HPrs to "1" and "2"). MAKE SURE YOU TURN DOWN THE GAIN FIRST WHEN MAING ANY EXPERIMENTAL FILTER CHANGES.

Hint 3: Notice that there is no Frequency setting on the Shape Generator used to modulate the oscillators. Sv only sets "W" for gating the shape generator on. The "F" column is empty. Formulas "A" and "C" use shape generator modulation by each other's formula. Try putting a "1" in the "F" column of Sv next to "W" and play. You will hear an overriding oscillation now controlling the creaking. You can set the value higher to increase that Low Frequency Oscillation. Try putting "Z" in the frequency slot instead to get pressure control of the overriding oscillation.

X: Pitch and cutoff control (with Y) - though this is so modulated a preset you don't hear much distinct pitch - more creaking.
Y: Controls both cutoff frequency and bandwidth of the high pass filters - higher frequencies coming out as you move to top of Y.
Z: Volume 

Macro i (Body): Sets convolution between 0..2 (using convolutions that move from bigger to smaller sound).

Cycle Kalimba:
Cycle Kalimba: A Harman using the "Kalimba Hard" spectral set is controlled with a variety of shape generator motion/cycling, particularly out of phase tremolo with controllable speed on the stereo outputs.

Note 1: This preset uses a fixed Convolution Response interpolation setting (".93" in the "Cna" column). ".93" here means the interpolation is 93% between 0 (Wood) and 1 (Metal) responses. Try changing this to other values to bring in another convolution setting ("2" for example to set to the full "Fiber" response in this case). You can get subtle changes in the sound this way. Note it also uses a "1" (100% wet) in the "M" (mix) column. This will apply the full convolution amount. This value can be changed - in a scaled range from 0..1. 

Note 2: Formula "F" in the "SR" column uses a shape generator modulation (sine-shape) based on Formula "M". "M" is Control controlled and moves from a min of ".25" to a max of "1.0" based on Macro ii (which also controls the speed of the modulation/tremolo). Formula E on "SL" also has a sine-based tremolo applied but it uses a fixed phase offset of ".25". Thus in addition to the tremolo speed control, Macro ii also controls shape generator phase offset change between the SL and SR stereo channels adding additional stereo motion.

Macro ii (TremSpeed): Controls the tremolo speed
Macro iv (Release): Controls sustain of sound after release through a blend of Persistence (formula "B").

FDN Crazyness: A noise waveshaped oscillator is sent through Feedback Delay Network of filtered taps, one of which also feeds back into the oscillator's waveshaping input for added complexity. A Saw WaveBank is also sent to the outputs to add an X-based frequency component to the sound (down 1 & 2 octaves from played pitch) which in turn is also used as a waveshaping input to the oscillator. All of this gets sent into the delay network resulting in one "'crazy'" mass of sound. 

Note 1: This preset uses the new "Tn" Delay tap function available on the single pole low pass filter ("LP1"). Notice that none of the Filters that are used to set up the delay network have any input (on triangle column). The new tapped delay function takes the Tap output from the Bank C delay (MicroDelay in this case) and applies that as input to the LP1 filter in the "Tn" column. HarMan - Basic:
Basic HarMan:  A building block preset for the Harmonic Manipulator. The Harmonic Manipulator can manipulate the spectra in predefined Spectral Sets, or Live data from the Delay module. These are very short samples but are not to be thought of as a samples as the spectral content is manipulated - a sample is not played. This is why a spectral set may not sound anything like its name when used in the Matrix. The short specral set is treated like a grain in granular processing. Harmonic Manipulators are in addition to Modal Manipulators which also manipulate Spectral Sets and Live data.

The current spectra sets available are Live (see note below), Bell, Drum, Kalimba Hard, Kalimba Soft, Marimba Hard, Marimba Soft, mBiraski, Metal, Spring, Noise 1, Noise 2, String Tap 1, 2 & 3, Viola Legato, Viola Marcato, Pizz. Loud, Pizz. Snap, Pizz. Soft, Spiccato Loud, Spiccato Soft, Alto Flute, Alto Sax, Brass, Clarinet 1 & 2, Flute 1 & 2, Oboe 1 & 2, Ukulele 1, 2 & 3, Toy Piano 1 Strike, Toy Piano 1 Release, Toy Piano 2 Strike, Crystal.

Parameters:
Harman Amplitude Input: Frequency domain interpretation: Amplitude of Harmonic Manipulator. If the amplitude is 0, no output is generated (conserves DSP processing). Time domain interpretation: Amplitude of grain, if a new grain is triggered. If the Amplitude is zero, no output is generated (conserved DSP processing).

Macro i (H): Harmonic Truncation. Frequency domain interpretation: Harmonic truncation, in kHz. More low harmonics will be truncated as H increases. Try .16 times the S column value. Time domain interpretation: Grain envelope step rate, if a new grain is triggered. Smaller H makes longer grains. Grain duration will be 1/H ms.
Macro ii (S): Spectral Dilation. Frequency domain interpretation: 1 means no change in spectral envelope, > 1 stretches the spectral envelope, < 1 compresses. Normally the S column and the H column differ only by a scale factor. Time domain interpretation: Step rate through grain source data, if a new grain is triggered. A value of 1 uses grain source data at original sample rate.
Macro iii (IRampSpeed): The Interpolation Between Spectra parameter is controlled with a single cycle ramping envelope, not Control controlled. This controls the ramping speed of that envelope. (You could add a Controll to better hear what that is doing instead of automatiing it with a SG.) 
Macro iv (RampMax): This is the max range of the ramp of the Interpolation between Spectra envelope control. 

Frequency domain interpretation: Interpolation between spectra selected in the Spectral Set popup menu. Value 0 to 1: 0 = first spectrum in the Set, 1 = last spectrum. Time domain interpretation, when "Live" is selected: Index into granulated data from Delay module. Additional values only for "Live": -1 = quantize starting point of grain source data to 2 * H, -2 = quantize only when S > 1.

Note:

fundamental, in kHz. Time domain interpretation: Controls how often a new grain is triggered:
trigger frequency in kHz. Add randomness to F for audible grain clusters.

Harmonic Board:
Harmonic Board: Play harmonic overtones (also high overtones whose frequencies are up to 5.5 octaves above the fundamental) of any pitch you play. Use your left hand to choose the fundamental, and your right hand to play overtones (harmonics) of this fundamental. The fundamental itself is actually muted and only the overtones are heard. 

Important details below:
As mentioned, the fundamental is played below the split point defined by Macro i (see below) using the left hand. NOTE: The fundamental should always be held down as the first note, and thereafter the overtones added while keeping the fundamental held down! Otherwise nothing is heard. 

It should be noted that the fundamental is monophonic, so you cannot play a chord but only a single note as the fundamental. But the overtones can be several at once, depending on your chosen polyphony.

Pre-9.9x Only: Macro i (SplitPoint) sets the position on the playing surface that corresponds to the fundamental. From then on, moving to the right, each half step corresponds to one higher harmonic.

Macro ii (Damping) determines how long each overtone keeps "ringing" after it has been played. In order for this to happen, 

Macro iii (Excitation) also has to be nonzero. This ringing is not limited by your polyphony setting, so using low damping values, it's possible to play huge chords of simultaneously sounding overtones by quickly playing many overtones in succession.

Playing an overtone at Y close to 0 reproduces it in its original octave. Playing at Y close to 0.5 shifts it down by 1 octave, and playing at Y close to 1 shifts it down by 2 octaves. Thus it is basically possible to play over a 3-octave range even if only 1 octave is available left of SplitPoint. So on a half-size Continuum, it would be convenient to choose F4 as SplitPoint if wanting to play overtones over a large range.
Due to the limited numbers of frequencies in the associated filters (there are 2 available BiqBanks, not 3), the excitation mentioned above has to be compromised, and can therefore be chosen in 2 ways. When 

Macro iv (ExcRange) is low (below about 64), all overtones up to the 48th will ring at Y=1 and Y=0, but only up to the 24th will ring at Y=0.5. Of the higher overtones at Y=0.5, only every 2nd will ring. When ExcRange is high (above about 64), all overtones up to the 48th will ring at Y=1 and Y=0.5, but only every 2nd overtone will ring at Y=0.

Control v (Mute) creates muting effect by adjusting BiqBank bandwidth.

This preset uses both BiqBanks at their higher setting, and therefore requires a bit higher processing power than many others. Note also that rounding has been enabled in this preset, but it's of course possible to switch it off. Overtones themselves are quantized, so it's not possible to play "in between" overtones (it would sound rather bad anyway).

Jenerator: A preset inspired by the Ondioline that lets you set three waveform settings with two filters in this case and ability to generate both tremolo and vibrato effects. Karplus - 1:
Karplus - 1:  A basic Karplus-Strong model.

From Wikipedia: "'Karplus-Strong string synthesis is a method of physical modelling synthesis that loops a short waveform through a filtered delay line to simulate the sound of a hammered or plucked string or some types of percussion. At first glance, this technique can be viewed as subtractive synthesis based on a feedback loop similar to that of a comb filter for z-transform analysis. However, it can also be viewed as the simplest class of wavetable-modification algorithms now known as digital waveguide synthesis, because the delay line acts to store one period of the signal. Alexander Strong invented the algorithm, and Kevin Karplus did the first analysis of how it worked.'" 

EaganMatrix Model: A low pass filtered noise pulse (single cycle shape generator pulse) is is sent into a fast (50 ms) VoiceDelay which then sets up a feedback loop where the delay signal is sent through a single pole high pass filter (very low frequency elimination) then into a steep (24 dB/Octave) single pole low pass filter to outputs and also fed back into the VoiceDelay feedback loop. So that initial pulse of noise is filtered and dies away. The Delay time is controlled by X (in formula B) as delay directly affects pitch/tuning. 

The physical model is meant to emulate a plucked string, where upon plucking you impart the string with a lot of engergy (noise burst) and then the high frequency component dies away faster than the low frequencies as the sound trails off (feedback loop through a low pass filter).

C. Duquesne, who created this preset, has a very instructive video on how Waveguide presets are created in the EaganMatrix with a detailed description of this preset. See: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xEv1Qybu16k

Macro i (inFilter): Controls the noise injecting low pass filter and feedback loop filter's cutoff frequency. Dampens at lower settings. 

X: Pitch
Y: Tone. Secondary control of the single pole feedback delay line's filter cutoff. More muted/damped on bottom of Y.

Kinetic Bowed FDN:
Kinetic Bowed FDN: A Feedback Delay-like Network triggered by a Kinetic Model bow createing a reverberant bowed metallic plate effect helped with the use of Analog Echo recirculation. 

Low pass filtered noise is single cycle down-ramped into  MicroDelay (never up-ramp noise into a feedback network or you may easily overload it). Each of the Four MicroDelay taps are controlled with their own time delay offsets and the taps are sent to alternating stereo channels as well as back into the feedback network. For the most basic building block this is based on, see the "'Utilities/Basic Karplus'" presets.

Note: In a WaveGuide-based preset such as this, changing the delay time of the MicroDelay taps can significantly change the pitch and Tone of the output.

Macro i (Damp): Damps the reverberation by controlling the delay time of all taps in parallel.
Macro ii (Release): Controls sustain after release by blending Persistence on all LP1s cutoff frequencies in parallel.
Macro iii (Spread): Affects perceived spread of the sound by changing the MicroDelay taps' delay time. Works in conjucntion with Macro iv.
Macro iv (Delta): A secondary offset control on the MicroDelay tap time delay. Works in conjunction with Macro iii.

v (Tune): Changes base frequency of the output by altering the frequency multiplier applied in parallel to all MicroDelay Taps' Delay times.
vi (Friction): Friction of there Bow.

Kinetic-Wavebank Morph:
Kinetic-Wavebank Morph: An example of how to easily morph between two sounds. A slightly modified "Bass Pad" preset was taken and modified to add a big Sawtooth Wavebank with it controlled by two formulas on the SL/SR column (E & H). These two formulas are set to a long Hann Shape Generator - each 180 degrees out of phase. Since they control the output volume as one sound is rising in volume the other is falling, thus creating a morph between them that is evened out a bit by also outputting the Phase Generator (that is used as the excitation input to the Kinetic Bank) under Z control at a lower volume. Additional Y control of the two sounds is added for more dynamic content.

Kyma 1:
Kyma Mode: Special Midi handling for Symbolic Sound Corporation's Kyma. 

This transmits a Midi message once per second to let Kyma know a Continuum Fingerboard is present.
Kyma will automatically update the Continuum Fingerboard when sounds are loaded and changed inside Kyma. Kyma-controlled Continuum Fingerboard parameters include: Polyphony"," X Bend"," Y Controller"," Z Controller"," and Splits.
  
All affected Kyma parameters will have blue text in the Continuum Editor.

Technical details: The Continuum Fingerboard will use controller 74 to encode Y"," controller 11 for Z"," and 96 for the pitch bend range. Splits in Kyma override the Continuum Fingerboard's split. In this special Kyma mode"," Continuum notes are transmitted on high-numbered Midi channels starting with channel "16".

Kyma will automatically update the Continuum Fingerboard when sounds are loaded and changed inside Kyma. Kyma-controlled Continuum Fingerboard parameters include: Polyphony"," X Bend"," Y Controller"," Z Controller"," and Splits.
  
All affected Kyma parameters will have blue text in the Continuum Editor.

Technical details: The Continuum Fingerboard will use controller 74 to encode Y"," controller 11 for Z"," and 96 for the pitch bend range. Splits in Kyma override the Continuum Fingerboard's split. In this special Kyma mode"," Continuum notes are transmitted on high-numbered Midi channels starting with channel "16".

Marlin Perkins 1:
Marlin Perkins 1: An African drum preset. A noise pulsed BiqBank is sent to stereo outputs with Z control of convolution response.

Note 1: This is a good teaching example for the use of the Bi-Quadratic Filter Bank (BiqBank). Here Y and Z are both used to assist in dynamically changing the BiqBank's parameters. attacking lightly without pressing down too far will get a crisp percussive sound. Pressing harder will bring out the noise component - especially if you keep your finger depressed.

Note 2 - Blend using a Formula: Note formula "E" on SL/SR. It uses a blend of Persistence based on a formula, not a Control or Gen that will manually raise the release/sustain. In this case it blends with formula "G", which is controlled by X in such a way that when X is low, more persistence is applied and when high, the sound dies away quickly (the value gets higher the lower you play and this the level of persistence increases). This makes the drum sound more realistic.

Metal Rainstick:
Metal Rainstick: A noise pulsed BiqBank (with controllable repeated attacks)is sent to the stereo outputs. The preset combines a noise based component with a resonant pitched component (when resonance is set high).

Note 1: This is another good preset for learning BiqBank usage. Start by placing the StrikeSpeed and SweepSpeed to "Stopped" and Resonance to "None". You can easily then hear how this preset moves from noise to a percussive strike - and then you can play with the Controls to easily hear what each does. When resonance is high, you just hear the noise component. When you bring resonance to full, at top of Y you can hear how the tones appear. 

Note 2: The overriding aspect of this preset are the repetitions. Shape Generator 1 is used to single cycle pulse the noise into the BiqBank. It uses a very quick pulse of 81 Hz (9x9). The trigger however is set to be controlled by shape generator 2 (formula "B") which is another pulsing function but controlled by Z - the deeper you press, the faster Svi's frequency becomes (up to a max of 50 times a second when Macro i is set to max). 

Also note that two BiqBank parameters are set to constants "sB" (Bandpass Bandwidth Spread) is set to ".8" and "sA" (Amplitude Spread) is set to ".1". Try changing these values to see how they affect the sound. For example, set "sB" to a low value of ".1" and you will create a more zither-like affect at the top of Y.

Finally because there is very little else going on in this preset, to better learn what kind of sounds you can get out of a BiqBank with a pulse of noise (a very common usage), remove all the formulas on the BiqBank Control and type in some values between 0 and 1 in each column (except the "F" column which you should keep at "X"). For example set "sF", "B", "sB", "C" and "sA" all to .40. You can still set "StrikeSpd" and "SweepSpd" Controls to control the repetitions. This will give you a noisy pipe sound. Set "sF" and "C" to ".8" leaving the others at ".4". This will become a lot more metallic a strike. Using this preset you can experiment now and get a good feel for what BiqBank parameter settings in this setting give you what timbre. (just don't set Bandwidth too low). MAKE SURE YOU TURN DOWN THE GAIN FIRST WHEN EXPERIMENTING WITH FILTERS.

Macro i   (StrikeSpd): Controls the speed of the repetitions. On lower Y this is more a flapping sound. On upper Y it is more a metallic strike.
Macro ii  (SweepSpd): Controls the retriggering of the noise pulse into the BiqBank. When this is set to "Stopped" the Biqbank is only triggered once.
Macro iii (Res): Controls filter resonance - bringing more pitched content in as it is increased. BiqBank Bandwidth in this case is actually affected by Macro iii in addition to X, Y and Z components.

X: Pitch 
Y: Timbre. Lower half of Y outputs more white noise, upper half a resonant strike. Totally controls Frequency Spread and contributes to bandwidth control.
Z: Volume + Timbre (BiqBank filter control).

Two very similar configured Harmonic Manipulators, one set to the "Sprong" spectral response (metal) and the other set to "Clarinet2" (reed) are sent to their respective SL/SR stereo channels. A bit of internal motion is applied through shape generator control of the Interpolation between spectra parameter of both HarMans.

Note: You can try morphing between other sounds by changing the spectral settings of the two HarMans. This may not produce great or expected results for some settings as the responses are in many cases highly affected by other HarMan parameter settings.

Macro i  (ToneSize): Affects Harmonic Truncation and Spectral Dilation of the HarMans. 
Macro iii (MetalSize): An offset only set on the "Sprong" (metallic) Harman that makes things a bitt less metallic sounding as the Macro increases (though the overall sound here is not totally metallic). 

X: Pitch
Y: Timbre control. As Y increases more metal is output and less reed (more reedy on the bottom of Y morphing to more metal on the top of Y).
Z: Volume and a secondary control of harmonic truncation.

Metallic Glass:
Metallic Glass: Vibraphone like model with metallic and glassy components including a rotor/oscillation function. Four oscillators set to inharmonic ratios are sent into a low pass filter to create the glassy sound. A ModMan set to Metal adds the metallic component. Finally a noise fed BiqBank set to main frequency is used to add further complexity to the sound.

Note: Look at formula G used as a multiplier on SL/SR that is affected by both shape generators to create the complex oscillation. Also try experimenting with changing W slightly in formulas A, B and C to different values that will create new inharmonic relationships in relation to the fundamental oscillator (OSC1) and change the glassy sound if you wish. 

Macro i (Rotor): Adjusts speed of main oscillation
Macro ii (FngrMot.): Speed of secondary "finger motion" applied with the main oscillation.

Metallic Pattern Gen:
Metallic Pattern Gen: A beat pattern generator. Two nearly identical noise-pulsed BiqBanks are output at different pulse intervals in such a way as to create a configurable pattern. You can set divisors of the main beat for each BiqBank from "1" to "12". Thus you can create beat patterns two against one, three against two, five against seven, etc. Just set the two divisors and any other parameters and press the fingerboard (since this does not use X, you can press anywhere). The two BiqBanks are set a bit different in timbre so you can hear the repeating pattern better.

Usage Hints: The Metallic Pattern generator can actually create some non-metallic sounds as well depending on the BiqBank parameters you set. It uses a fixed base pulse speed (because at the multiple of 12 things get repeated about as fast as you can perceive). If you want to speed up or slow down the base rate, set "W" in formulas "A" and "C" to the same value (these control the shape generator base speed). BE SURE TO SET THEM THE SAME OR THE GENERATOR WILL PRODUCE DIFFERENT RESULTS. 

If you want to add dynamic pitch control as you play on X, in the "F" Frequency Column, under formula F, add "X" in the "+" or "-" rows. This will not map to the exact frequency on he fingerboard but you will be able to play pitches. For an interesting dynamic pitch difference, place "X" on the "+" row underneath formula "F" on one BiqBank and place it on the "-" row under formula "F" on the other.

Macro i   (Divisor-V1): Sets division of the beat for the first beat generator from 1 (basic division) to 12 (12 times the base beat interval).
Macro ii  (Divisor-V2): Sets division of the beat for the second beat generator tone from 1 (basic division) to 12 (12 times the base beat interval).
Macro iii (Freq): Pitch control. Controls Frequency of first bandpass filter.
Macro iv  (Spread): Pitch control. Controls Frequency Spread. 
v (Bandwidth): For Timbre control. Varies Bandwidth.

Mini Shepard Breathing:
Mini Shepard Breathing: Emulates a constantly rising Shepard Tone (with a flute like quality) by sending two sine waves with adjustable upward ramps 180 degrees out of phase - as the waveshaping inputs to another sine wave sent to the outputs. A separate single pole low pass filtered noise component is sent to the outputs to simulate a bit of breathing.

Note 1: The "'Dry'" Control when set to its full amount may force you to reduce gain as the L/R outputs have a multiplier on them (constant 4 in the X row under the L/R columns). If you want a less maximum dry sound, reduce those constants - say to 2.

Note 2: This preset also uses a Shape Generator (Hann) motion on convolution (formula B) which cycles the convolution response at Svi speed back and forth through the (0..1) responses - Guitar-Metal in this case. 

Macro i (Tone): Controls amount of waveshaping input into the main oscillator. Because only sine waves are used waveshapers of another sine tone, the resulting sound never gets too crazy sounding and maintain a certain sine tone characteristic.
Macro ii (Dry): Increases the amount of output to the unprocessed (L/R) outputs (see formula H) - thus making he sound drier as the recirulator contributes less and less effect. Note that this is balances by using a ".1" multiplier on the SL/SR outputs in the Z row (if too much processed sound would be sent the Dry setting would not be as noticeable).
Macro iii (Speed): Speed of the ramping. If this gets too fast you don't really hear a Shepard-tone like motion (and this preset is not meant to emulate a pure Shepard's tone as you can always hear when the repetions recycle.

X: Pitch

Mini Shepard Resonant:
Mini Shepard Resonant: A Shepard-tone inspired preset with full resonant sound enhanced by the use of a Modulated Delay Recirculator. This uses a similar technique as in Mini Shepard Breathing but instead of ramping two sine oscillators 180 degrees out of phase with each other, here four sine wave oscillators are ramped 90 degrees out of phase with each other and used to waveshape a fifth oscillator which in turn is sent as the input to a BiqBank which is sent to the SL/SR outputs.

Note: To better hear what each ramping component is doing, diable formulas D, G and H in OSC 5's input column and then bring them back in one at a time. 

Macro i  (Tone): Controls the waveshaping inputs in parallel.
Macro ii (Speed): Controls ramping speed, but because four oscillators are now used all out of phase, the ramping is less noticeable - more a pulsing.
Macro iv (Pitch): Changes the base pitch by changing the frequency first bandpass filter of the BiqBank. X still operates as usual on each of the driving oscillators.

Mini Shepard:
Mini Shepard: The simplest of the "'Mini Shepard'" presets - and the one the other two ("'Mini Shepard Breathing'" and "'Mini Shepard Resonant'")are built on. Simulates a continually rising "'Shepard'" tone by ramping two sine tone 180 degrees out of phase with each other and using them to waveshape a third sine wave oscillator.

Note 1: This preset does not use any speed control. The Shape Generator #1 ramping frequency that controls the motion is set at "'02'" (will complete a ramp cycle every 50 seconds). Change this to a faster value if you want a faster ramp time (or better create a Control control for this value).

Note 2: Because the output uses the standard Z pressure function, you will not get a constant amplitude on the outputs and this will create an inconsistency in the sound that somewhat breaks the traditional Shepard tone effect. You will create a better simulation by turning this into a drone preset (one that starts playing immediately without any fingerboard interaction). To do this replace the standard Z formulas on the SL/SR OSC 3 outputs with a constant of "'.1". Just in case you make a mistake, turn down the gain before experimenting.

Macro i (Tone): Alters the waveshaping input amplitude with out of phase Hann waveforms on each of the inputs to add more motion.

ModMan - Pulsed:
Basic ModMan Pulsed: A basic preset to experiment with the Modal Manipulator. This is similar to the Harmonic Manipulator but instead of simply controlling the HarMan input amplitude, the ModMan is typically excited - often by a pulse or ramp of noise. Here the ModMan is set to spectral set "'Vla Spic. Soft'" and excited with a pulse of filtered noise. Changing the Frequency spread will create all kinds of struck and or plucked sounds. From there you can experiment with Bandwidth. The lower you set it the more resonance and the more the sound will ring out and sustain. The other Controls and dials control the remaining ModMan parameters. Their affect on he sound will vary.

Also note that this preset is set to the quadratic options. You can try setting to sF (Spread Frequency) and sB (Spread Bandwidth) and the sound becomes stronger, more percussive and less delicate. Turn down the gain before experimenting here. YOU can also set sF to the last option sA (Spread amplitude). This will soften up the sound in this case.

For ModMan, a popup menu allows you to select a predefined Spectral Set to load into the Delay memory, or Live to manipulate spectral envelope data (spectral period "620.69" Hz) you record into the SummedDelay.

The Deflation Limit (above the last ModMan matrix column) avoids excessive buildup of energy inside the ModMan, but has no effect under normal playing conditions. Set the Deflation Limit to the largest value (between 0 and 7) that does not affect the timbre of the sound. Click on the Deflation Limit to change its value. Note: When you select a Spectral Set, it occupies half the memory of the VoiceDelay, SummedDelay, MicroDelay, and FormulaDelay. If you have one Manipulator with Spectral Set (in Bank A or Bank B), you can also have a VoiceDelay, SummedDelay, MicroDelay, and FormulaDelay in Bank C (which will operate using half its normal memory). If you have two Manipulators (both Bank A and Bank B) as well as a Delay in Bank C, both Manipulators must specify the same Spectral Set.

Macro i (QuadSpread): (qF-Quadratic) Spread Frequency. Select  sF=1 for harmonic spacing of modes, >1 stretched, <1 compressed. qF times mode-number-squared is each mode's frequency offset. sA>0 reduces amplitude of modes farther from Centre
Macro ii (BandCtrl): Mode Bandwidth Control. Bandpass bandwidth, smaller values increase mode resonance.
Macro iii (SprdBand): (Quadratic) Spread Bandwidth. sB>0 increase bandwidth farther from Centre (see below), <0 decrease. qB times distance-from-Center-squared is bandwidth offset.
Macro iv (Center): Center Control. Value in range 0 to 1. 0 means first mode is Centre, 1 means the 8th mode is Centre.
v (Interpret): Interpolation between Spectra. Interpolation between spectra selected in the Spectral Set popup menu. Value 0 to 1: 0 = first spectrum in the Set, 1 = last spectrum.
vi (SpecDial): Spectral Dilation. 1 for unchanged spectral envelope, >1 stretched, <1 compressed. Normally the S and H columns differ only by a scale factor.

X: ModMan Frequency - Frequency (in kHz) for the first mode in the ModMan.
Y: Tone/Drive. Controls cutoff of filtered noise going into the ModMan. At bottom of Y to mid Y filter is set to X. Above that it is set to "2.5 times x". In this case more high frequency noise will excite the ModMan and it will have the effect of increasing the drive as well as slightly alter tone.
Z: Not Used. This preset uses a fixed volume based on the initial noise pulse. Volume will change based on what Frequency Spread and bandwidth you have set and also Y setting that changes filtered noise excitation.

Mojo of FDN:
Mojo of FDN: A Waveguide-based Feedback Delay-like Network creates a reverberant plucked metallic string effect helped with the use of Analog Echo recirculation. 

Low pass filtered noise is single cycle down-ramped into  MicroDelay (never up-ramp noise into a feedback network or you may easily overload it). Each of the Four MicroDelay taps are controlled with their own time delay offsets and the taps are sent to alternating stereo channels as well as back into the feedback network. For the most basic building block this is based on, see the "'Utilities/Basic Karplus'" presets.

Note: In a WaveGuide-based preset such as this, changing the delay time of the MicroDelay taps can significantly change the pitch and Tone of the output.

Macro i (Damp): Damps the reverberation by controlling the delay time of all taps in parallel.
Macro ii (Release): Controls sustain after release by blending Persistence on all LP1s cutoff frequencies in parallel.
Macro iii (Spread): Affects perceived spread of the sound by changing the MicroDelay taps' delay time. Works in conjucntion with Macro iv.
Macro iv (Delta): A secondary offset control on the MicroDelay tap time delay. Works in conjunction with Macro iii.
v (Tune): Changes base frequency of the output by altering the frequency multiplier applied in parallel to all MicroDelay Taps' Delay times.

X: Pitch

Morphing Church Organ:
Morphing Church Organ: Similar to Morphing Organ only this adds a Triangle Wavebank duplicating the Oscillator waves for added sonic effect. An organ model that morphs the harmonic content using a set of shape generators to add four random partials each at a different rate. The speed of the partial generation can be controlled to create a glassy effect. A sub-base tone an octave below the fundamental can be added with a control. The tuning of the partials can be offset as well with another control. More an effect preset than an organ to play normally.
 
X: Pitch
Y: Not Used
Z: Volume

Pedals: Ped1 set to control Rate of harmonic change. Ped2 set to bring in the sub-bass tone based on the BassTone setting.

Macro i (HarmRate): Adjusts the rate at which the random partials are added.
Macro ii (SubBase): Adjusts the amount of an oscillating sine-like base is added an octave beneath the fundamental.
Macro iii (Detune): Allows the random partials to be detuned/offset to give a more complex sound.
Macro iv (BassTone): Adjusts the bass tone (None, 2 octave beneath fundamental, 1 octave beneath fundamental or 5th beneath fundamental).

Note 1: Try changing the Integrated Oscillators to DSF in any combination you like and changing the Wavebank type to Saw or Square. You can adjust the strength of the added partials by altering Z range in formulas S, T, U and V. Manually adjust the recirulator controls for the Echo as desired.

Note 2: You can change the distribution of partials created by changing W values in formulas A, C, E, and G. If you set the Ancillary Quantize function in these formulas to Multiply, you will create inharmonic partials for a more glassy effect.

Morphing Reed:
Morphing Reed: A preset that can take on a variety of reed-like timbres. A "master" oscillator is sent in parallel through four different filters with different cascade settings. Those filters are morphed using shape generators at different speeds to dynamically change their frequency settings (not too drastically).
 
X: Pitch
Y: Secondary morphing between filters (in addition to the dynamic SG-based morphing)
Z: Volume + Filter bandwidth control

Macro i (Timbre): Adjusts the Spectral Balance (timbre) of the master oscillator.
Macro ii (Delay): Adjusts the delay amount.
Macro iii (SelfMod): Brings in a bit of self-modulation on the Master oscillator that creates a somewhat brighter sound.
Macro iv (Echo): Adjusts the echo amount. Note: if you want no echo, set the Recirculator Mix to Dry in the Recirculator controls - or bring it down if there is too much default echo for your taste.
v(Body): Moves through a full range of convolution settings: Fiber-Wood-Metal-Waterphone.
vi(Breath): Brings in a bit of BiqBank filters noise to add a breathy component if you wish.

Morphing Voice:
Morphing Voice: A simple preset that morphs a BiqMouth into a SineSpray as you move from bottom to top of Y. Initially set to similar timbres but two controls allow you two set them more apart from each other for more drastic morphing.
 
X: Pitch
Y: Morph. Uses two inverted S shape curves on Y to smoothly morph between BiqMouth at bottom of Y to SineSpray at Top of Y. 
Z: Volume

Macro i (VocShape): Lets you scroll through the BiqMouth shapes in steps of 0.1.
Macro ii (Timbre1): Controls timbre of BiqMouth by changing formant frequency offset.
Macro iii (Timbre2): Controls timbre of SineSpray by changing sinusoid grain frequency.
Macro iv (Intensity): Adds more Voice component by increasing the BiqMouth input using a secondary Oscillator whose spectral balance is also increased as BiqMouth Timbre1 increases. Note that the BiqMouth is primarily driven by the SineSpray as input so there is a bit of control loop going on there.
v: (WahSpeed): The SineSpray has a Single Cycle SG on its Harmonic Truncation and Sinusoid Frequency controls whose SG frequency is controlled by v. This creates a filter-like "Wah" initial attack. This control shortens the "Wah" envelope as it is increased. In effect it gives the SineSpray a bit of a vocal character as well.
vi: (Body): Convolution control for additional timbre change that takes things through Wood->Metal->Fiber->Snap convolutions. 

Note 1: Try changing The Y shape in formulas C and D to create different Morphing elisions. YOU can adjust Z in formula J to increase or decrease the BiqMouth vocal affect if you don't like the ratio imposed by the Intensity control.
Morphing Wavebank Pad 1:
Morphing Wavebank Pad 1: A variation of Morphing WaveBank Pad 1 with slower resposne and more complexity. 

A very dynamic preset that moves in and out of two timbres, rather organ like at times but also with subtle shifting background noise. Uses two WaveBanks each emphasizing different octave ranges with SG volume control 180 degrees out of phase to smoothly alternate/elide the two timbres. In addition they are sent into Low Pass and High Pass filters that also shift in and out. Two Oscillators with different spectral balance are also sent into a multiplier and added to the output for a low level static component that is also is rotated in and out to add to the dynamic and somewhat random sound that results as everything has a Hann shape generation on it including separate dynamic convolution motion on each WaveBank as well. Note: Not ideal for ContinuuMini due to the Y manipulation that may cause discontinuities (some may like that). In any case, it is a somewhat unpredictable preset in timbre and range due to all the dynamic SG control.

Also note that most of the Shape Generators use a constant, not W gate for triggering. This means the SGs are always active and the sound will not start at a predictable timbre. If you want to always have the sound start at the same point replace the "1s" with "Ws" in the Shape Generator's "T" input.
 
X: Pitch
Y: Timber shift. Changes Amplitude weighting of the WaveBanks. Also affects bandwidth of the filters.
Z: Volume

Macro i (ConvLev): Increases the amount of Convolution range. The Convolution and recirculator both have dynamic SG motion on them for additional timbre shifting. 

Note 1: Try changing the Wavebank types to change the morphing timbres. Also try changing Convolution types for the first two options (note some settings can become quite loud).

Note 2: The Analog Recirculator used has a noise component that will be heard in the background after the sound dies away if Convolution or Recirulation level is set high enough. If you want to remove that either turn down the Convolution Control or pull the Noise Macro in the recirculator down.

Eight note polyphony MPE, using 14-bit encoding for Y and Z.
Uses Midi Channel 1 as Master Channel, and Midi Channels 2-9 for notes.

W: Midi KeyOn is sent when finger initially touches surface, KeyOff when finger is lifted.

Z: Pressure is encoded using encoded with controllers "70" (most significant) and "102" (least significant, when nonzero).

For Y and Z, the Continuum sends least significant then most significant data.  To avoid MPE's 14-bit update glitches, the receiver should wait to use the least significant bits until the most significant bits are received.  If no least significant bits are sent, assume "0".

RPN "0" is used to transmit the bend range, and will reflect any changes you make to the Bend Range in the Continuum Editor.
To use MPE's "Strike" value with KeyOn (instead of encoding all the pressure trajectory of the attack), select "Key Velocity" in the Note Processing menu.
Mr Kyte:
Mr Kyte: A multi-modulated preset where a foreground sine-like controlled pitch motion and background quantized pitch motion are combined. An oscillator with Hann shaped LFO modulation of its spectral balance and a second oscillator with similar spectral balance control but also with LFO-based phase modulation and a triangle shaped pitch quantization are used to waveshape a third oscillator with X controlled spectral balance. The output is sent through a low pass filter that is totally controlled by Z. This creates multiple levels of modulation.

Note: In modulated presets such as this, it can be instructive to listen to the individual modulating sources. Try disabling the preset Z formula in the SL/SR columns on OSC/Filter row "4". Place the Zs on SL/SR OSC/Filter row 2 instead to hear the first modulating source. That will give you the foreground pulsing component. Now disable that and place the Zs on SL/SR OSC/Filter row 3 to hear the second modulating source. That will give you the Up/Down (triangle) ramping quantized component (achieved by formula F - a quantized pitch multiplier). Finally, disable those Zs and now place the Zs on SL/SR OSC/Filter row 1 to hear the waveshaped modulated result before passing the the low pass filter.

Macro i (Speed): Controls the relative speed of both the foreground and background motions in parallel.

X: Pitch
Y: Not Used
Z: Volume + Tone (controls filter cutoff and bandwidth)

Mutable Bowl:
Mutable Bowl: Shape generator modulated low pass and band pass filtered noise is fed into a BiqGraph (Mode Amplitudes) Bank with scaled A1 and A2 amplitude offsets controlled by Y and Z respectively. The result produces a range of variable glass-like sounds.

Note: This is a good example to examine how the BiqGraph Graph function works. Click the "Graph" text under the "BiqGraph1" entry. You will see three graphs. The Main "Mode Amplitudes" graph on the left that affects the bas scaling of harmonics of the input to the BiqGraph module. Then there are the "A1" Scaled Offsets" and "A2 Scaled Offsets" that get applied as harmonic dB amplitude offsets to the "Mode Amplitudes" graph depending on the  value of column "1A" and "2A" (note a new feature not used in this case also allows you to scale %frequency and bandwidth adjustments by selecting "1F" or "2B").

Two very simple formulas are used ("B") to control the value of "1A" offsets and ("F") to control the values of "2A" offsets. Formula "B" is totally controlled by Y motion and formula "F" by Z motion. Looking at the "A1 Scaled Offsets", as Y goes from 0 to ".41" in formula "B", the Mode Amplitudes harmonic #1 is greatly reduced and #2 greatly increased (and harmonic #3 is reduced just a bit). A much more complicated set of offsets are applies as Z pressure moves from 0 to ".31". To better hear what this does to the sound (FIRST TURN DOWN THE GAIN), bring up formula "B". This goes to a max of "0.41". Play and listen to the sound. Now increase Y to go from "0" to "1.0". You should easily be able to hear how the A1 offsets are now applied to their full percentage (not max of 41%) and the metallic sound at top of Y is really evident due to the great emphasis of the second harmonic.

Macro i   (Mute): Lessens sustain and mutes the sound. Affects Bandwidth. Lessens resonance as Macro increases which has effect of less sustain and muting.
Macro ii  (Body): Controls Convolution range 0 to "0.75". Thus the convolution range is not great ("0"=Snap, "1"=Guitar). Also note the convolution length of the guitar response is set low ("21").
Macro iii (Fret.Buzz): Controls amount of noise fed into the BiqGraph from the Band Pass Filter. When this is set to zero the Band Pass filter does not contribute to the resulting sound.

Octavator:
Octavator:  An sine oscillator that changes octave based on voice number is used to phase modulate another sine oscillator which is sent to outputs and also into a tapped delay loop. Modulated delay is also applied creating a massive reverberating octave shifting effect.

Note: This preset is a good study in how Voice number can be used to dynamically change preset parameters. Look at formula B that controls the octave switching. W is set to 12 times the Voice number (offset from X which is set OCT). Thus based on voice prority (Oldest here), the voice number will change each time the fingerboard is pressed cycling in oldest priorty through voices 1 through 5 (Base 5 is set in this case). Finally the Ancillary formula mods W with E (36) so the octave don't get to high - and the entire formula is translated back to note Number (NN) from Octave format in the Ancillary section.

Osc - Formula Delay:
Basic Formula Delay:  The FormulaDelay provides a method of creating long delay times for control data used with EaganMatrix under formula control. This preset is a simple example for study and to use as a building block. Unlike the Voice Delay and Summed Delay whose delay times range from 50 milliseconds to 6.4 seconds, the Formula Delay has delay range of .45 seconds to 57.6 seconds.

The FormulaDelay provides four delay buffers for each voice, for delaying control data used in Matrix formulas. Typical values to feed through a FormulaDelay might be X, Y, Z, or a pedal. The FormulaDelay is available in Bank C. No output from FormulaDelay appears directly on matrix rows; instead, the delay buffer outputs (T1, T2, T3 and T4) are available by selecting Buffer 1..4 in the W component of formulas.

For each of the four possible delay buffers, the FormulaDelay takes:  Buffer Input (triangle): Input to FormulaDelay's first delay buffer. This buffer's output is available by selecting Buffer 1 in the W component of a formula and Delay for Buffer: Delay time for FormulaDelay's delay buffer 1. 0 = no delay, 1 = max delay (selected in the Delay menu).

The Delay popup menu has a choice of maximum delay times for the FormulaDelay. The sample rate of FormulaDelay's delay memory is normally at the formula evaluation rate (1 kHz), but it can be limited by two variables: maximum delay and polyphony. Very long delays or high polyphony may result in reduced sample rate for the delay memory. Consider filtering or slewing the data inputs to FormulaDelay when using long delay times in the Delay popup menu, to avoid aliasing the control signals being delayed through FormulaDelay.

Note: When a WaveBank or Manipulator with Spectral Set is in use (in Bank A or Bank B), the FormulaDelay will still operate, using half the normal amount of delay memory.

In this preset, only one FormulaDelay buffer is used and it is set to the lowest (".45" second) delay option. Notice formula B that is used as the frequency offset control for OSC1 (X is set in formula A) and also as an amplitude offset to Macro input into the delay. Formula C controls the delay time for the first buffer through pressure/Z. First disable formula B in the FormulaDelay input column and play. You will hear the triggered note and its delay. Trying setting the Formula Delay to "1.8" seconds to hear it well. Turn back on the delay's formula B. Because the delay Buffer in Formula B is also used to scale input back into the delay (how to set up a FormulaDelay loop), when you press you will hear a series of ascending notes whose speed is dependent on pressure due to formula C.

Osc - Sine Wave:
Basic Sine Wave:  The basic building block and starting point to learning the Eagan Matrix. Here a Digital Summing Formula (DSF) oscillator set using X as frequency without the Spectral Balance parameter being set. This produces a sine-like tone.

Oscillator notes: 
Each Oscillator has three columns:
Audio Input: Oscillator 1 phase modulation input, 0 = 0 radians, 1 = 2? radians. Use this for modulation or waveshaping, or as a seed value for Noise from Seed. Leave this blank for an oscillator without modulation.

Frequency: Oscillator 1 frequency control, in kHz. Leave this blank for a waveshaper, and for Noise from Seed.

Spectral Balance: Oscillator 1 spectral balance, 0 for pure sine, >0 to add harmonics, 1 for max harmonic amplitudes. For waveshaping, this provides a continuous real-time control of the nonlinear filter's transfer function.

A number of different Oscillator types are available:
Select Normal DSF for harmonic amplitudes that decrease with harmonic number in an exponential fashion determined by the S column. 

Select Integrated DSF for harmonic amplitudes proportional to the inverse of harmonic number; S=0.8 has the same harmonic amplitudes as a sawtooth. (Refer to the graphs below for Normal DSF and Integrated DSF waveforms.) 

Select Phase Generator to output the oscillator's 7 internal phase generators, with the S column controlling frequency spread in Hz. Expose Phase is equivalent to a sum of 7 non-bandlimited sawtooth waveforms (for bandlimited saws, see "WaveBank"). 

Select Noise from Seed for a random noise generator based on a seed value. If the same seed value is used for each note (a constant in the triangle input column and W in the T column), the sequence of random numbers will be the same for each note.

Note. The Res(onance) Macro is programmed so that as you raise it the value decreases (resonance increases as bandwidth value decreases). Look at formula F. It starts at W="-1.9" with a Y constant offset of "-0.050" - but also with an Ancillary offset of "+2". So at minimum Res Control setting the value will be "1.95" and when you increase the Control the value will decrease - thus increasing Resonance. When programming filters, be careful to make sure you avoid the bandwidth from going to zero (or very close to it) which will normally cause the filter to ring, possibly uncontrollably. Remember to turn down the gain when experimenting with filters if you are not sure of results.

Random Trigger: A BiqBank simulates a randomly bouncing object using a random trigger (formula A) on the shape generator that controls BiqBank input and Frequency Spread. Digital Echo with high pass filter is applied to create the reverberation.

Note 1: A good example on how to turn a control on and off at a random rate. The random trigger is created by using an Ancillary formula B on the main trigger formula A. SineSpray - Basic:
Basic SineSpray: A sine grain generator. The sine spray is granular like the HarMan is granular, just the sine spray granulates an artificially produced sine wave as opposed to the harmonic manipulator which granulates a very short recording.  The grains are most "normally" 2-period long grains, windowed with a Hamming window.  So if you use HarMan granular to pitch shift a sound by 0 half steps - in other words play it back at original frequency -- you have two overlapping grains all the time.  A grain is triggered once each synthesis period - but the grain length (window length) is 2 periods - so always 2 grains playing.  If you pitch shift down an octave using granular, only one grain plays at a time - that's because the synthesis period is now twice as long as the original period, and you are only triggering one grain each synthesis period. 

Similarly if you pitch shift up an octave using granular, four grains play all the time, since the synthesis period is half as long as the original period. So if you use a sine spray to play back a pure sine wave (not particularly useful), you will actually be using 2 grains overlapping all the time.

The SineSpray takes an amplitude setting as the first parameter, not an audio input. If the amplitude is 0, no spray is generated
(conserves DSP processing).

Macro i (FundFreq): Adjusts the Frequency of Sine Spray's fundamental, in kHz. It is common to add randomness to this value to create audible clusters within the Sine Spray.

Macro ii (HarmTrunc): Harmonic truncation, in kHz. Small H creates long sine grains within the spray. Larger H shortens the grains and adds harmonics. As H increases, high harmonics increase and low harmonics get truncated. Try half the S
column value.

Macro iii (PhaseOff): Phase offset for sinusoid within the Spray.

Macro iv (SineFeq): Frequency for sinusoid within the Spray, in kHz.

X: Affects speed of repetitions
Y: Affects speed and timbre (but depends on Control settings as will have little effect for some settings).

Sub-Harmonic Generator:
Sub-Harmonic Generator:  This preset emulates the Sub-Harmonic generator section of a Mixtur-Trautonium. You can set four subharmonics. 1=1st Harmonic, 2=1st overtone beneath first harmonic, 3= 2nd overtone beneath the 1st harmonic, etc. In other words the overtones series in reverse, beneath the fundamental instead of above it. A SideTone can also be added and full timbre control (though the Mixtur-Trautonium uses sawtooth waves).

Note 1: The relative amplitudes of each of the subharmonics and Side-Tone are set in decreasing order in the formulas in SL/SR - all based on different maximum Z settings in formulas (V, U, T, S, and M). If you want to change the relative amplitude of them change the ending pint of Z in each of these formulas.

Note 2: Fixed convolution response is set in the Metal range using Length control. You can play around with different values as you like.

Note 3: You can set the Side-Tone to a different WaveBank option if you would prefer it to be a Sawtooth or Square wave.

Synth Lead 3:
Synth Lead 3: A triangle wave based synth preset.   A Triangle WaveBank set to a chord is sent to outputs and also into a SummedDelay feedback loop with Modulated Delay recirculation (with sine LFO modulation applied to the Recirculator Time parameter).

Note: This preset uses a common technique to create a chord from a WaveBank using formula component X's Zero Point setting. The X component has a Zero Point, which is the position on the Continuum surface where the X component of the formula has an output of zero (for Continuous and Initial mode). In a pitch sense, this is where Middle C will be. X will normally default to C5. There is a selection in the X formula to set Zero Point Pitch and Zero Point Octave. What happens if we create a formula and change X's Zero point to Ab4? This means if you play the Ab beneath middle C, middle C will now be played. Now let's set a WaveBank to play one wave with X=default C5 and one wave with X=Ab4. If you play middle C on the fingerboard, the expected default X function will play middle C, but the wave set zero point to Ab4 is now transposed up a major third from where it would have played middle C. The major third (E) above middle C is played as a result. In this manner we can set different zero points on waves in a wavebank to get expected chords.

Three waves are used in the "'SynthLead 3'" preset. The first (r1) using the default X parameter which will play expected pitches on the of Ab3. If a C is played, using the function described above, this will play E6 - a major 10th above the played note. The third wave (r3 - Formula A) sets the Zero Point to F4. This will play (G5) a fifth above the played note.

You can reset the zero points to play any desired chord related to default C5 zero point. Here are some options for setting Zero Point X formula values of waves in a WaveBank to play different triads and seventh chords (of course you can change their zero point octave to create different spacings):

Major: r1=X, r2=Ab4, r3=F4
Minor: r1=X, r2=A4, r3=F4
Diminished: r1=X, r2=A4, r3=F#4
Augmented: r1=X, r2=Ab4, r3=E4
Dominant 7th: r1=X, r2=Ab4, r3=F4, r4=D4
Major 7th: r1=X, r2=Ab4, r3=F4, r4=C#4
Minor 7th: r1=X, r2=A4, r3=F4, r4=D4
Half Diminished 7th: r1=X, r2=A4, r3=F#4, r4=D4
Fully Diminished 7th: r1=X, r2=A4, r3=F#4, r4=Eb4
Major-Minor 7th: r1=X, r2=Ab, r3=F4, r4=C#4
etc.

Synthetic Cathedral:
Synthetic Cathedral: A big resonant filtered multi-octave oscillator preset. Two oscillators set to sine wave, one two octaves below the other are sent to the outputs. A Phase Generator oscillator with Z-based timbre Macro is sent into a low pass filter to the outputs and also into a tapped SummedDelay feedback loop with the two taps sent to opposite stereo channel with different delays to get the nice stereo effect which is enhanced by using a Modulated Delay recirculator.

Note: This preset has a very nice stereo delay effect that is enhanced by using two techniques. Notice formula A that is used as an offset to the base ".90" constant applied to the "'D'" delay column in the SummedDelay. The "'.90'" means 90% of the 400ms delay will be applied and the other 10% is taken care of by adding formula A to it. Formula A applies a bit of sine LFO modulation to the total which adds some presence to the sound. Disable formula A to hear what that change contributes.

The other delay technique involves the use of the two delay taps T1 and T2 that are sent in the SL/SR column to opposite stereo channels. Although both use the same formula (G) to output the tap, the configuration of the two taps use different delay percentages (T1 = 1 and T2 = ".50"). This will add some stereo motion to the sound to make it more alive. Try setting SummedDelay T2 column from its current value of ".50" to 1 to be the same as the T1. As this moves through the delay loop you can hear something special was removed from the stereo sound by using the same delay percentage.

A Modulated Delay also adds the reverberant sitar-like sympathetic string effect.

Note 1: Try light taps with this preset as well as slides. Setting the HarMan to "'Vla Legato'" also creates a nice effect. 

Note 2: The main initial sustain of this preset develops through the use of a very long single cycle shape generator down-ramp (10 seconds on Sv) that is applied SL/SR outputs on Formula C. Notice that Formula C uses Ancillary formula O which is triggered on Sv W as Trigger gate. Also notice in formula C that Z does not begin at 0, but at a slight offset. This means that background sound is always preset and on gate in formula C, the sound will come in with a long ramp down even if you just quickly tap. Try changing the ".1" in Sv Frequency ("'F'") column to 1. The ramp will now die away in a second and the effect will be lost. Likewise, if you change Z in formula C to start at "0.00" instead of "0.04", the whole sitar effect falls apart. Small changes in the EaganMatrix can have big results.

Tick Tube:
Tick Tube: A noise pulsed BiqBank is sent to the outputs.

Note 1: A simple example of how to use a noise controlled BiqBank. Notice Formula A uses a single cycle shape generator (Svi set to Pulse) to send a pulse of noise into the BiqBank. The pulsing is repeated as you hold your finger down because the frequency of Svi is triggered by Sv which is a continuous pulse. Remember the Shape Generator is Triggered when the "T" column goes from 0 to some positive value. The Sv continuous pulse function thus constantly triggers the single cycle Svi. This technique is used in a number of system presets.

The BiqBank's Frequency Spread and Bandwidth parameters are controlled by a combination of Y and Z. Thus as you move Y from front to back and press harder you will change the sound from a more noise attack to a resonant tube sound (as you press harder resonance is decreased giving you the more pitched sound and Y increases frequency as you move from front to back). You can see how the Continuum can seamlessly integrate its surface Macro into a sound. 

Note 2: The base frequency of the BiqBank is set two octaves down from X ("F" column set to the .25 constant multiplier). TURN DOWN THE GAIN. Try setting this to .5 and then to 1 (or disable the constant). This will raise the base frequency for the first bandpass filter in the BiqBank and create a much more metallic sound. You can also try setting the Spread Frequency from "sf" to Quadratic "qF". This will create an even more metallic sound (no longer a tube effect).

Uki Pizz 1:
Uki Pizz1: A Harmonic Manipulator set to the "'Ukulele1'" spectral set is sent through a single pole high pass filter. A quick tap will create a pizzicato that has a nice trailing release.

Note 1: This preset uses two single cycle shape generators to control the basic plucking sound. The first (Svi) is a rather slow down ramp placed on the SL/SR column (formula D) to control the envelope of the entire output. If you press, the sound will eventually die away. The second (Sv) is a quick up ramp placed on the Interpolation Between Spectra parameter of the HarMan. This is what creates the plucking timbre. Try changing the Sv's "'F'" column from 5 (times a second) to 1. This will widen the pluck. Now try changing it to 9. This will tighten the pluck as the ramping sped is almost doubled. Try creating a Control to change this value allowing you to shape the size of the pluck. Now try changing formula A in the Harman's "'I'" column to a constant - say ".4". The SG is here removed and the plucking disappears. Envelope control through shape generators is very important in creating pluck/struck effects. ALWAYS TURN DOWN THE GAIN BEFORE EXPERIMENTING. 

Macro iv (Release): Controls sustain after release on the Harman amplitude using blend of Persistence.

Voice Jumper:
Voice Jumper: A dual wave shaped Oscillator (OSC2) is sent to SL/SR and also into a BiqBank which is in turn sent through two dynamically controlled all pass filters each sent out opposite stereo channels. Voice Number Macro is used on a number of parameters - hence Voice Jumper.

Note 1: The two All Pass Filters applied to the BiqBank output are set to opposite ramping functions each sent to a different L/R stereo output. This add a big stereo pulsing effect on top of the base repetition caused by the shape generator (Svi) control of the BiqBank Frequency Spread. Try disabling the "Z" outputs in SL/SR on OSC 4/5 and set "Z" on SL/SR for Bank A output. This will allow you to hear what the pulsating/ramping all pass filters add to the sound.

Note 2: There are two shape generators used, one set with a multiplier of .25 versus the other with the same trigger. This will cause one to move four times the speed of the other. Formula J is used at the trigger and this is set Ancillary to use Voice 1's WXYZ components. Sv ramps the All Pass Filter control and Svi ramps the BiqBank Frequency Spread for every four ramps of the APFs. This creates that 1-2-3-4 pulsing effect where 1 in the pattern is accentuated (the Frequency Spread repetition).

Furthermore the frequency of OSC3 uand the Spectral Balance (timbre) OSC1 both used to waveshape OSC2 are controlled by Voice Number.

Z: Volume + affects amount of waveshaping of OSC2.

Macro ii (Depth): Affects the depth of shape generator ramping of the cutoff frequency for All pass filters and Spread Frequency the BiqBank.
